transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

I came in because I keep hearing these voices, like clear as if somebody’s standing right there in my little studio. It’ll be quiet, nobody there, and I hear them saying my name and saying my work is being judged. And I know how that sounds, but it’s not like the TV left on or somebody outside—my neighbor does bang around sometimes, she’s always moving furniture or something—but this is different. It feels right there with me, and it’s been really upsetting.
Around the time the voices started, did you also have a period where you felt unusually energized or high?

Yeah… yes, I did. It’s like I’d get this feeling like I was bright, like everything was opening up and Greenville couldn’t even hold all the plans I had in my head. Like I was chosen for something, you know? And then real quick I’d flip—somebody would ask me a little thing, like a client asking me to repeat myself, and I’d just snap hard at them. Then later I’d be thinking, why did I get so mad over that?
Had you been using any drugs around the time the voices started?

Drugs? I mean… I don’t really know how to answer that. I wasn’t thinking about it like that at the time. People say “drugs” and I think of folks hanging around the corner near the bus stop, and I’m not like that—I’m usually just trying to get to work and keep my apartment together. But around when it started, I’m not sure what all counts or what you mean exactly.
Before the voices started, had you used meth, cocaine, cannabis, LSD, or taken pills that weren’t prescribed to you?

I… I don’t know. I mean, I know the names you’re saying, but I can’t really line it up in my head like that. Before the voices started, I was just trying to get through my shifts and get home, and people offer things sometimes, or talk about things, but I don’t want to say yes to something if I’m not sure. 

Pills too, I mean, everybody has pills in their cabinet, my aunt used to keep all hers in a little butter cookie tin, you know those blue tins? But for me… I can’t really give you a clear answer on those specific things.
How long have you been hearing the voices?

About… about nine months, I think. It started and then it just didn’t really leave. The voices, and that feeling like my work is being watched—like somebody’s keeping track of me there. 

Nine months is what I keep coming back to, though. I remember because I was still trying to keep my schedule straight, and time gets funny when you’re tired, but… yeah, around nine months now.
Did the voices begin while you were using any street drugs or pills not prescribed to you?

I’m not really sure, doctor. I keep trying to put it in order, like “this happened, then that happened,” but it’s all kind of mixed up in my head. I know you’re asking if it was like street drugs or somebody else’s pills right when the voices started, but I can’t give you a clean yes or no.

Back then I was mostly thinking about work and getting through the day. People talk about stuff, people offer things sometimes, and then you got family with medicine bottles everywhere—I remember my aunt had so many little bottles lined up, and she’d get mad if anybody touched them—but for me, I don’t know that I can say the voices began while I was using anything like that. I just don’t have it clear enough.
Have you found yourself caring much less than usual about things like seeing people, work, or basic daily tasks?

Yeah… I think so. When I’m not all wound up, I can just kind of sit there for hours, with my coffee sitting right next to me getting cold. I’ll hear the phone and just… not answer it. 

I used to go to the walking club sometimes, you know, those ladies with the matching sneakers, they’d always talk about whose knees were bad—but I haven’t been going. And my paintbrushes are right there, I can see them, and I just don’t even care to pick one up. It’s like everything feels too far away.
Have the voices ever continued during a time when your mood felt normal—not especially high, energized, irritable, or depressed?

Yeah… yes, I think that did happen. There was a stretch after I wasn’t so… revved up, I guess. My energy had dropped back down, and I was sleeping more like a regular person again—not all over the place.

But the voices didn’t stop then. They kept on for weeks, and I still had that feeling at work like people were judging what I was doing, or keeping track of me somehow. Like even when my mood felt more normal, that part was still there.

It’s hard to explain because when you’re working in people’s homes, everybody does watch how you do things a little—like if you fold towels wrong or put the cups in the wrong cabinet, they notice—but this felt like more than that. It kept going even when I didn’t feel especially up or down.
Was there ever a period of at least two weeks when you were hearing the voices even though your mood was otherwise normal?

Yes… yes, there was. After that time when my energy kind of came down and I wasn’t staying up so much—like I was sleeping more normal, making breakfast at a normal hour, not rearranging things in the middle of the night—the voices were still there.

It wasn’t just a day or two. It went on for several weeks, I think. And I still had that feeling at work, like people were judging what I was doing or keeping track of me somehow. You know, in home care people do notice little things—where you put the towels, if you wiped the counter right—but this felt like more than that. Even when my mood wasn’t especially high or low, it kept going.
Have you had a period of at least two weeks when you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day?

I don’t know… depressed like that, most of the day every day for two weeks, I’m not sure I can say that. I have days where I feel real low and heavy, like even getting dressed feels like too much, but then I’ll get distracted by something, or I’ll have to go do for somebody else, and it’s not the same all day.

Two weeks is hard for me to count. I don’t keep track good. I’ll think it was a whole month and then my sister says, “No, that was last Tuesday,” so… I don’t want to tell you wrong.
During these past nine months, have you ever had a time when you felt sad or empty most of the day nearly every day for at least two weeks?

I’m not really sure about that. I know I’ve felt sad, yeah, and empty sometimes, but “most of the day nearly every day” is hard for me to say.

Sometimes I think it’s been going on forever, but then the days all run together, especially when I’m working and going from one person’s house to another. Like one lady I help, she keeps all her mail stacked on the kitchen chair, and I’ll be thinking about that instead of how I feel, you know?

So… I don’t want to say yes if I’m not sure. I’ve had low days, but I can’t tell you it was two straight weeks like that.
During this past year, was there ever a time when you needed much less sleep than usual and still felt full of energy?

Yeah… yes, that did happen. There were nights I only slept maybe two or three hours, and then I’d get up like I’d had a whole night’s rest, just charged up.

I’d go right back to painting, or I’d start making calls, like it was a normal time to be doing all that. And I remember thinking, well, if I’m awake I might as well get things done… but it was a lot of nights like that, not just one.
Before the voices started, did you have any seizure, head injury, or other serious medical illness?

I don’t know… I mean, not that I remember. I didn’t have, like, some big accident or anything that sticks out to me before all that.

I’ve bumped my head plenty of times, you know, everybody does—cabinet doors, car doors, one time at work I hit it on a shelf reaching for towels—but I don’t know if that counts. Nobody told me it was serious. And seizures… I don’t think so. I’m not sure what all counts as a seizure, though.
During the past nine months, was there ever a time when you lost interest in almost everything you usually enjoy for at least two weeks?

I don’t really know how to measure that. I mean, there’s times I don’t feel like doing things, but then I might still sit there with the TV on or mess with my paints a little, or I’ll think about doing it and not actually do it.

Two weeks is the part I get stuck on. Because with my work, the days kind of blend together, and I’ll be at one house helping somebody with their bath or their lunch, and then I come home and it’s already late, and I think, well, maybe I didn’t enjoy anything, but maybe I was just tired.

So… I can’t say for sure that I lost interest in almost everything for two whole weeks. I don’t know.
During the times you felt unusually energized and needed very little sleep, were you using meth, cocaine, cannabis, LSD, or pills that weren’t prescribed to you?

Um… I don’t really know. I mean, I wasn’t thinking of it like that at the time, like checking off what I had or hadn’t used.

Pills, I’m careful about because people offer you things sometimes, you know, like at work somebody says, “Oh this helped my back,” and I have back pain from lifting folks, but I don’t like taking random stuff. And cannabis, meth, cocaine… I don’t know, I don’t want to say the wrong thing.

Those times I was up, I just remember being up and feeling like I had to keep moving. I can’t really tie it to something like that for sure.
During the past nine months, was there ever a time when you felt depressed nearly every day for at least two weeks?

I don’t know… depressed is a big word, you know? Like, I get down, sure, but nearly every day for two weeks, I’m not sure how I’d even count that.

Some days I’m just worn out from people needing me all day, and then I go home and sit there, and I think maybe I’m sad, maybe I’m just tired. And then another day I might be talking to somebody at the store about tomatoes or the price of eggs, and I seem fine for a minute.

So… I can’t really say yes to that. I don’t know if it was two weeks like that.
Before the voices began, were you diagnosed with any serious medical illness?

Before the voices… I don’t know. I mean, I’ve been to doctors here and there, mostly when something gets bad enough that I can’t ignore it, like you know how people say “go get that checked” and then you put it off because you got work and somebody’s mother needs help getting dressed, and then the bus is late…

But a serious illness? I’m not sure what counts as serious. I don’t remember anyone sitting me down and saying something like that before all that started. At least not that I can say for sure.
Have you used cannabis?

Cannabis… I mean, people talk about it like it’s nothing now, like everybody’s got gummies or somebody’s nephew grows it, and I hear that a lot at work, especially when folks are hurting or can’t sleep.

For me, I don’t really keep track of it like that. I’m not saying yes exactly, I just… I don’t know what you’re counting. Like smoke? edibles? being around it? I’ve been around people using it, sure, but I can’t give you a clean answer.
Was there ever a full month when you were hearing the voices while your mood felt normal?

Yeah… I think so. Not like I was happy-happy, but my mood wasn’t doing that big up-and-down thing. After my energy came down and I was sleeping more like a regular person, the voices didn’t just stop.

They kept going, and I still had that feeling like people were watching how I did my work, judging me, maybe keeping track of things. That went on for several weeks, I think. It’s hard to pin down, because work weeks all run together, and there’s always somebody needing help with their shoes or their medicine or whatnot… but yes, there was a stretch where my mood felt more normal and that stuff was still there.
Before the past nine months, had you ever heard voices like this before?

Before the past nine months… I don’t think I heard them like this before. Not like clear, like somebody standing right there in my little studio, you know? Saying my name, telling me my work is being judged.

I mean, sometimes you think you hear something when the TV’s low or the pipes make noise, and my neighbor upstairs walks heavy, drops things like she’s moving furniture at midnight… but this is different. This is when the house is quiet and nobody’s there, and I still hear it clear.

patient.answer:
Yeah… yes, that did happen. There were nights I only slept maybe two or three hours, and then I’d get up like I’d had a whole night’s rest, just charged up.

I’d go right back to painting, or I’d start making calls, like it was a normal time to be doing all that. And I remember thinking, well, if I’m awake I might as well get things done… but it was a lot of nights like that, not just one.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms could be due to a medical condition rather than a primary psychotic disorder.
doctor.question: Before the voices started, did you have any seizure, head injury, or other serious medical illness?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about possible medical or neurological causes before the voices began, such as seizures, head injury, or serious illness, which is not covered by the symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I don’t know… I mean, not that I remember. I didn’t have, like, some big accident or anything that sticks out to me before all that.

I’ve bumped my head plenty of times, you know, everybody does—cabinet doors, car doors, one time at work I hit it on a shelf reaching for towels—but I don’t know if that counts. Nobody told me it was serious. And seizures… I don’t think so. I’m not sure what all counts as a seizure, though.

inference.note: Two+ weeks of hallucinations/delusions with euthymic mood plus clear decreased need for sleep/energized periods supports schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type more specifically than F25.9. Schizophrenia/unspecified psychosis remain possible; substance/medical causes not ruled out by history.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been a major depressive episode, which would help distinguish schizoaffective disorder from schizophrenia-spectrum psychosis.
doctor.question: During the past nine months, was there ever a time when you lost interest in almost everything you usually enjoy for at least two weeks?

target_item.reason: The question asks about loss of interest or pleasure in almost everything for at least two weeks, which is a depressive symptom. The provided profile does not include a specific depressive anhedonia item, and the closest negative-symptom item is not directly about a two-week depressive episode criterion.

patient.answer:
I don’t really know how to measure that. I mean, there’s times I don’t feel like doing things, but then I might still sit there with the TV on or mess with my paints a little, or I’ll think about doing it and not actually do it.

Two weeks is the part I get stuck on. Because with my work, the days kind of blend together, and I’ll be at one house helping somebody with their bath or their lunch, and then I come home and it’s already late, and I think, well, maybe I didn’t enjoy anything, but maybe I was just tired.

So… I can’t say for sure that I lost interest in almost everything for two whole weeks. I don’t know.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has ever been a manic episode independent of substance use, which would help distinguish schizoaffective disorder from substance-induced psychotic disorder and other schizophrenia-spectrum diagnoses.
doctor.question: During the times you felt unusually energized and needed very little sleep, were you using meth, cocaine, cannabis, LSD, or pills that weren’t prescribed to you?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about possible substance or non-prescribed medication use during energized, low-sleep periods, and the provided symptom profile does not include substance use or medication-induced symptoms.

patient.answer:
Um… I don’t really know. I mean, I wasn’t thinking of it like that at the time, like checking off what I had or hadn’t used.

Pills, I’m careful about because people offer you things sometimes, you know, like at work somebody says, “Oh this helped my back,” and I have back pain from lifting folks, but I don’t like taking random stuff. And cannabis, meth, cocaine… I don’t know, I don’t want to say the wrong thing.

Those times I was up, I just remember being up and feeling like I had to keep moving. I can’t really tie it to something like that for sure.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has ever been a major depressive episode, to distinguish schizoaffective disorder from schizophrenia spectrum disorders.
doctor.question: During the past nine months, was there ever a time when you felt depressed nearly every day for at least two weeks?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a depressive mood episode, specifically feeling depressed nearly every day for at least two weeks. The provided symptom profile does not include a depressive mood symptom item, so no listed item directly covers this.

patient.answer:
I don’t know… depressed is a big word, you know? Like, I get down, sure, but nearly every day for two weeks, I’m not sure how I’d even count that.

Some days I’m just worn out from people needing me all day, and then I go home and sit there, and I think maybe I’m sad, maybe I’m just tired. And then another day I might be talking to somebody at the store about tomatoes or the price of eggs, and I seem fine for a minute.

So… I can’t really say yes to that. I don’t know if it was two weeks like that.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether the psychosis could be due to a medical condition by checking for a temporal relation to a serious medical illness around onset.
doctor.question: Before the voices began, were you diagnosed with any serious medical illness?

target_item.reason: The question asks about whether a serious medical illness was diagnosed before the voices began, but the symptom profile does not include medical illness history or medical causes.

patient.answer:
Before the voices… I don’t know. I mean, I’ve been to doctors here and there, mostly when something gets bad enough that I can’t ignore it, like you know how people say “go get that checked” and then you put it off because you got work and somebody’s mother needs help getting dressed, and then the bus is late…

But a serious illness? I’m not sure what counts as serious. I don’t remember anyone sitting me down and saying something like that before all that started. At least not that I can say for sure.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has a history of substance use that could explain the psychosis, helping distinguish primary psychotic disorders from substance-induced psychosis.
doctor.question: Have you used cannabis?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically about cannabis/substance use, which is not covered by any item in the symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Cannabis… I mean, people talk about it like it’s nothing now, like everybody’s got gummies or somebody’s nephew grows it, and I hear that a lot at work, especially when folks are hurting or can’t sleep.

For me, I don’t really keep track of it like that. I’m not saying yes exactly, I just… I don’t know what you’re counting. Like smoke? edibles? being around it? I’ve been around people using it, sure, but I can’t give you a clean answer.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there was any psychosis for at least one month without prominent mood symptoms, to distinguish schizoaffective disorder from schizophrenia/other psychotic disorders.
doctor.question: Was there ever a full month when you were hearing the voices while your mood felt normal?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 3
target_item.manifestation: There was a time after my energy dropped and I was sleeping more normally when the voices and the belief that people were judging or tracking my work kept going for several weeks.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether hallucinations continued for an extended period while mood felt normal, which directly matches psychotic symptoms occurring without a major mood episode.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think so. Not like I was happy-happy, but my mood wasn’t doing that big up-and-down thing. After my energy came down and I was sleeping more like a regular person, the voices didn’t just stop.

They kept going, and I still had that feeling like people were watching how I did my work, judging me, maybe keeping track of things. That went on for several weeks, I think. It’s hard to pin down, because work weeks all run together, and there’s always somebody needing help with their shoes or their medicine or whatnot… but yes, there was a stretch where my mood felt more normal and that stuff was still there.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is a clear history of non-bizarre psychotic symptoms without prominent mood episodes, supporting schizophrenia over schizoaffective disorder or unspecified psychosis.
doctor.question: Before the past nine months, had you ever heard voices like this before?

target_item.name: Hallucinations
target_item.manifestation: I came in because I keep hearing voices clear as somebody standing in my little studio, saying my name and telling me my work is being judged, even when the house is quiet and nobody is there.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the patient had heard voices like this before the past nine months, which directly concerns hallucinations.

patient.answer:
Before the past nine months… I don’t think I heard them like this before. Not like clear, like somebody standing right there in my little studio, you know? Saying my name, telling me my work is being judged.

I mean, sometimes you think you hear something when the TV’s low or the pipes make noise, and my neighbor upstairs walks heavy, drops things like she’s moving furniture at midnight… but this is different. This is when the house is quiet and nobody’s there, and I still hear it clear.

opening_question.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has persistent psychotic symptoms for about 9 months, including auditory hallucinations and persecutory/judgment-related ideas. There is also evidence of a manic syndrome with decreased need for sleep, elevated/expansive mood, increased energy, grandiosity, and irritability. Critically, psychotic symptoms continued for several weeks to at least a month while mood was reportedly normal, supporting schizoaffective disorder, manic type, over schizophrenia or unspecified psychosis. Substance-induced psychosis cannot be confirmed because substance timing/use remained unclear, and no clear medical etiology was established.
